consensus_summary: The consensus primary meaning is the Garden of Eden as paradise: place of God’s presence, abundance, and unbroken human communion, lost by the Fall and restored in the new creation (with complementary layers such as temple, bride/Church, fruitfulness, or Gethsemane).
book_summary: The book defines garden as a planted stand of trees that symbolizes a grouping of nations.
consensus_core_identification: Eden/paradise (divine presence and fellowship, lost and restored)
book_core_identification: planted stand of trees = grouping of nations
boundary_disagreement: Book abandons the Edenic-paradise cases entirely as the core referent and reassigns the term to national collectives via tree imagery, so the consensus boundary of divine-communion settings is not refined but replaced.
material_contradiction: Consensus core (garden = Edenic place of communion) and book core (garden = grouping of nations) cannot both be true of the same referent in the same sense; accepting the book requires rejecting the paradise identification.
rationale: Minimum cores are irreconcilable: every consensus response centers on Eden/paradise (lost/restored) as the settled primary sense, with listed alternatives remaining complementary. The book’s ‘planted stand of trees — grouping of nations’ is absent from both primary and alternative lists, replaces rather than narrows or overlaps that referent, and is explicitly flagged by the book itself as departing from the common paradise teaching.
strongest_objection: Ezek 31:9 still embeds the trees inside ‘the garden of God’ and ‘trees of Eden,’ preserving the paradise frame; the trees (not the garden) are the nations, so the verse does not redefine garden itself as a national grouping.
